papers_read.title_as_printed: Deep learning combining FDG-PET and neurocognitive data accurately predicts MCI conversion to Alzheimer's dementia 3-year post MCI diagnosis (Cao et al., Neurobiology of Disease 187 (2023) 106310)
18F-FDG-PET Radiomics Based on White Matter Predicts The Progression of Mild Cognitive Impairment to Alzheimer Disease: A Machine Learning Study (Peng et al., Acad Radiol 2023; 30:1874-1884)

what_each_reports.P-81: ADNI 164 sMCI / 93 pMCI, conversion within 3 years of MCI diagnosis, 5-fold CV (Table 3): whole-brain FDG-PET 3D CNN alone AUC 0.6102 +- 0.0231 (BA 0.5651); five cognitive scores (CDRSB, LDEL, MMSE, mPACCdigit, mPACCtrailsB) alone AUC 0.7496 +- 0.0683 (BA 0.7130); PET+Age+CS AUC 0.7849 +- 0.0963 (BA 0.7326). Authors: 'neurocognitive scores predict better than PET per se', noting some scores were used in the AD diagnosis.
what_each_reports.P-88: ADNI-2/GO 341 MCI (102 progressed during up to 8-year follow-up), time-ordered split 238/103 (Table 3): white-matter FDG-PET radiomics signature AUC 0.747 train / 0.719 test; ADAS 0.755 / 0.742; CDR 0.683 / 0.737; SVM integrated model 0.868 / 0.865. Mean FDG SUV was not an independent predictor on multivariate regression. Authors state the rad-score was superior to clinical scale scores, but their Table 3 shows ADAS AUC at or above the signature in both groups; DeLong testing is reported only for the integrated model.

quantity_a: 3-year MCI-to-AD conversion discrimination (ROC-AUC, 5-fold CV) of (i) a 3D CNN on whole-brain FDG-PET and (ii) a network on a 5-score cognitive composite, ADNI-1/2/GO.
quantity_b: MCI-to-AD progression over follow-up of up to 8 years, discrimination (ROC-AUC, time-split test set) of (i) a 10-feature white-matter FDG-PET radiomics signature and (ii) single clinical scales (ADAS, CDR), ADNI-2/GO.
incompatible_if_same: Weakly at most. The contested ordering is 'cognitive scores vs FDG-PET alone'. P-81 finds cognition clearly ahead (0.75 vs 0.61). P-88's own numbers put ADAS slightly ahead of or level with the PET signature (0.742 vs 0.719 test; 0.755 vs 0.747 train), with no test of that difference. So on the printed numbers both studies lean the same way, and only P-88's verbal claim of PET superiority, unsupported by its table, points the other way.

gates.task: match in outline: MCI-to-AD conversion prediction (T2), but horizons differ (fixed 3 years vs progression at any point in up to 8 years).
gates.dataset_family: match: both ADNI (P-81 ADNI-1/2/GO, P-88 ADNI-2/GO); participants likely overlap in part.
gates.validation_tier: match: both internal only (5-fold CV vs a time-ordered internal split); neither external.
gates.modality_family: match on the imaging arm (FDG-PET) and the cognitive arm (clinical/neuropsychological scores), but the PET input representation (whole-brain voxels in a CNN vs white-matter radiomics texture features) and the cognitive predictor set (5-score composite vs single ADAS or CDR) differ.

endpoint_and_metric: incompatible endpoint: P-81 uses conversion within 3 years; P-88 uses conversion at any time during an 8-year follow-up. Metric type (ROC-AUC) matches. Predictor sets differ on both arms.
performance_validity: flag does not apply: no value near 0.97 in the conversion task (P-81's 1.0 values are its CN vs AD pretraining, which the authors attribute to circularity, and are not part of this comparison).
independence: Distinct author groups; both use ADNI MCI participants, so the cohorts partly overlap (not quantifiable from the papers).
grounds: The endpoint horizon differs: P-81 predicts conversion within three years, P-88 progression during an eight-year follow-up.

The FDG-PET predictor differs in representation (whole-brain voxel CNN vs a white-matter radiomics signature) and the cognitive predictor differs in content (a five-score composite vs single ADAS or CDR scales).

On the numbers actually printed, both studies put cognitive scores at or above PET alone; the only opposing element is P-88's verbal claim of radiomics superiority, which its own Table 3 does not bear out and which was not tested.

evidence_quotes.quote: FDG-PET and CS were obtained at MCI diagnosis to predict AD conversion within three years of MCI diagnosis using convolutional neural networks.
It is not surprising that the neurocognitive data together predicted better than FDG-PET per se because some of the neurocognitive data were used in the diagnosis of AD.
We analyzed the data of 341 MCI patients from the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative, of whom 102 progressed to AD during an 8-year follow-up.
We also found that the rad-score was superior to clinical scale scores (Fig 5C, 5D)

record_defects: claim_b 'FDG-PET hypometabolism alone achieves AUC 0.79': P-88's PET-only signature has AUC 0.747 (train) / 0.719 (test), and it is a white-matter radiomics texture signature, not hypometabolism; mean FDG SUV was not an independent predictor (multivariate NA).
claim_a 'AUC 0.77' for cognitive scores: P-81 reports 0.7496 for cognitive scores alone and 0.7849 for PET+Age+CS.
resolution_note 'overlap in cohort (N=89) but different evaluation periods': neither paper reports an N of 89 or a shared subset; the difference is the prediction horizon (3 years vs up to 8 years).
The listed 'bridging evidence' papers are unrelated headline scores and do not explain the pair.
what_would_change_the_verdict: A same-horizon comparison in which P-88's PET signature significantly outperformed the same cognitive composite P-81 used (or vice versa by a margin excluding the other's estimate) would make this a comparable ordering claim; with the printed numbers it would then still lean to false_positive, since both studies show cognition at or above PET alone.
